newsitem.title: ITALY: Serb power struggle outcome can affect peace--US.
newsitem.headline: Serb power struggle outcome can affect peace--US.

text.p: The U.S. ambassador to the United Nations said on Wednesday that Washington supported Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic in her fateful power struggle with ultra-nationalists, including indicted war criminals.
"The key question now facing all of us is how to support President Plavsic while simultaneously preventing her removal...," Ambassador Bill Richardson said in Rome after a trip to former Yugoslavia.

"The outcome of this political struggle is going to have profound implications on Dayton, on the peace process. So our efforts should be united...," he told reporters after meeting Italian leaders. He did not spell out what effects he expected.
Bosnian Serb hardliners expelled Plavsic from the ruling party on Saturday and demanded she step down from office.
The Serb Democratic Party (SDS), which rules Bosnia's Serb entity, is dominated by ultra-nationalists loyal to former president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic.
"Mainly I was there to show our support for her current situation. We discussed some aid. We support the constitutionality of her position...she is in a difficult situation," Richardson said.
The vote to kick Plavsic out of the party followed her outspoken attacks on Karadzic at rallies and her comments in an interview threatening to arrest Karadzic and his allies for rampant corruption.

"She is going to get help. We, the United States, are going to give her some help for her local community and I suspect other countries will contribute. We have to stand behind her. She is a strong woman," Richardson said.
The envoy said he expected the American aid to go through next week. He gave no details of the amount or type of aid.
The expulsion of Plavsic from the party does not affect her legal position as president. The constitution requires parliament to call a referendum to remove the president.

Richardson said that during his meeting with Plavsic he stressed the importance the United States attached to the Dayton peace process in Bosnia, now divided into Serb and Moslem-Croat entities loosely linked by a multi-ethnic presidency.
Another priority stressed to Plavsic, he said, was the return of refugees to areas now ruled by authorities which drove them out during the 1992-95 war.
"...We want more progress. At the same time she is facing a political crisis and we want to show support for her."

Serb hardliners have accused Plavsic of being too cooperative with international mediators who also want to arrest Karadzic and other indicted Serbs for trial by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.
The U.S. envoy also said Croatian President Franjo Tudjman had "agreed, stated his willingness, to ensure that the Bosnian Croats indicted for war crimes are sent to The Hague to stand trial.
"But most importantly he (Tudjman) agreed that all (refugee) Croatian Serbs willing to abide by Croatian law are now welcome to return to Croatia," Richardson said.
